what: The browser HTTP cache stores responses and reuses them, guided by headers such as Cache-Control and ETag. Give hashed asset files a one-year immutable lifetime and make HTML revalidate, and repeat visits are fast while deploys still show up at once.
like: Like keeping a printed timetable in your bag: fine until it expires, then you ask the office 'has it changed?' and they just say 'no, same one' instead of reprinting it.
why: Repeat visits load assets from disk with no network
Revalidation with a 304 saves bandwidth when nothing changed
Hashed filenames let you cache for a year yet ship fixes instantly

steps.d: The build puts a content hash in the filename (app.3f9a.js). When the content changes the URL changes, so the old cache entry is simply never asked for again.
Send Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable. The browser reuses the file without even asking the server.
The HTML name never changes, so use Cache-Control: no-cache (often with private). The browser stores it but checks before each reuse.
The request carries If-None-Match with the stored ETag. If nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, and the cached copy is fresh again.
A deploy changes the hashes inside the new HTML, so users get new files at once while unchanged files stay cached.

numbers.l: seconds (one year) in max-age for hashed static assets, with immutable
Not Modified: a body-less reply that marks the cached copy fresh again
of the time since Last-Modified is the typical heuristic freshness when no explicit lifetime is given

choices.d: no-cache stores the response but must revalidate before reuse. no-store forbids storing and also loses benefits like the back/forward cache. MDN prefers no-cache with private for personalised pages.
Long max-age with immutable only works when the URL changes with the content. HTML cannot be cache-busted, so it revalidates.
private keeps a response to the user's own browser cache; public allows storing even with an Authorization header. Use private for user-specific data.
max-age=1, stale-while-revalidate=59 serves a stale copy at once and refreshes in the background. Browsers without support ignore it and use max-age.

instead.why: When you need offline support or full control of caching in code
To cache at the edge, closer to many users, on top of the browser cache

breaks.d: The browser guesses freshness from Last-Modified.
breaks.see: Users see stale content for unpredictable times
breaks.fix: Set Cache-Control explicitly on every response

breaks.t: Long cache on a fixed filename
breaks.d: app.js has max-age of a year but the name never changes.
breaks.see: Users stay on an old build after deploy
breaks.fix: Content-hash filenames for long-lived assets; revalidate everything else

breaks.d: An old HTML page points at asset hashes that no longer exist.
breaks.see: 404s or a broken page right after a deploy
breaks.fix: Serve HTML with no-cache, and keep old hashed files available for a while

say: Hashed assets get Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, so repeat visits cost no network.
HTML gets no-cache with an ETag, so every visit revalidates cheaply with a 304 and deploys show up immediately.
I set Cache-Control explicitly on every response, use no-store only for truly sensitive data, and keep Vary narrow.

followups.q: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
followups.a: no-cache lets the browser store the response but forces a check with the server before reuse. no-store means do not store it at all.
Browsers revalidate more on reload; immutable tells them not to bother for assets that will never change.
It creates a separate cache entry for almost every browser string. MDN advises private instead of varying on Cookie.

today: The modern recipe is stable: content-hashed assets with a year-long immutable lifetime, revalidating HTML, and stale-while-revalidate for data that can be slightly old. RFC 9111 is the current caching specification, and service workers sit on top when you need offline control.

check.why: The URL changes when content changes, so a year-long cache is safe.

check.a: The cached copy is still valid; no body is sent
check.why: It validates the stored response and refreshes its freshness.

check.a: Store it, but revalidate before every reuse
